faqs.answer: 15 g of coffee to 240 g of water at 1:16. That is about 3 level tablespoons of ground coffee, though a scale is more reliable than a spoon.
faqs.question: How much coffee do I need for one cup of pour-over?

faqs.answer: 1:16 is the standard starting point, and most roasters work between 1:15 and 1:17. Start at 1:16, brew it three times, then move one step stronger or lighter to suit your taste.
faqs.question: What is the best ratio for pour-over coffee?

faqs.answer: Sour usually means under-extraction: the water was too cool, the grind was too coarse, or the brew ran too fast. Check the water is 92 to 96 C, grind a little finer, and aim for a three-minute brew.

howToSteps.name: Weigh the coffee
howToSteps.text: Use 15 g of coffee for one cup, or scale up at 1:16. Grind it medium-fine, like coarse sand.

howToSteps.name: Heat the water
howToSteps.text: Bring the kettle to the boil, then let it sit for about 30 seconds so the water falls to 92 to 96 C. Rinse the paper filter with hot water and tip the rinse water away.

howToSteps.name: Bloom the grounds
howToSteps.text: Put the coffee in the dripper and pour about twice its weight in water over it. Wait 30 seconds while the grounds swell and release gas.

howToSteps.name: Pour and wait
howToSteps.text: Pour the rest of the water in slow circles, keeping the water level steady. The brew should finish in about three minutes. Take the dripper off and the coffee is ready.

title: Pour-Over Coffee to Water Ratio
tutorial: Pour-over is the most forgiving way to learn ratios, because the maths is the whole recipe. One gram of coffee for every 16 grams of water. Weigh the coffee, multiply by 16, and that is your water. A single cup is 15 g of coffee and 240 g of water, which is an 8 oz mug.

The 1:16 starting point sits inside the range most specialty roasters use, 1:15 to 1:17. Go to 1:15 when you want a bolder cup or you are brewing a dark roast. Go to 1:17 for a lighter cup, or for a light roast where you want the brighter notes to come through. Change the ratio one step at a time and brew the same coffee three times before you decide.

Water temperature matters as much as the ratio. The Specialty Coffee Association puts the brewing range at 92 to 96 C, which is 200 to 205 F, or about 30 seconds off the boil. Cooler water under-extracts and tastes sour. Boiling water scalds the grounds and tastes bitter. A kettle with a thermometer takes the guessing out of it.

Grind medium-fine, like coarse sand, and give the grounds a bloom: pour just enough water to wet them, about twice the coffee weight, and wait 30 seconds while the gas escapes. Then pour the rest in slow circles. The whole brew should take about three minutes from the first pour to the last drip.

One thing that surprises people: the cup holds less than the water you pour. Spent grounds hold back about twice their weight in water, so 240 g of water over 15 g of coffee gives you about 210 ml in the mug. The calculator shows that yield, so you can pour a little extra water when you want a full mug.
